Centrioles. These are cylindrical, membrane-free structures made of nine triplets of microtubules arranged in a perfect nine-fold symmetric pattern. Usually you find them in pairs, and when they're together they form what's called a centrosome or microtubule organizing center—the MTOC. This pairing anchors and nucleates the formation of microtubules that organize the entire cytoskeleton and the spindle fibers that pull chromosomes apart during cell division. Most animal cells have them, though plant cells and many other organisms don't.

The nine triplet microtubules are the real signature here—each triplet consists of three fused microtubules bound together. When a centrosome forms, you get a pair of centrioles surrounded by something called pericentriolar material. Within that material sit gamma-tubulin ring complexes that actually nucleate the polymerization of microtubules growing outward.

During cell division, the centrosome duplicates during the S phase, and then the duplicated centrosomes move to opposite poles during mitosis to organize the spindle. But centrioles have another role too. They can be modified into something called basal bodies, which serve as anchors for cilia and flagella on the cell surface.

The duplication of centrioles follows a template-based assembly process that ensures each new cell receives its own MTOC. Interestingly, centriole duplication occurs only once per cell cycle, maintaining this precision through cell generations. Mutations or amplification of centrosomes can lead to chromosomal instability, which is particularly important in cancer cells.
